label: Type 2 diabetic, frightened by family history, quietly under-controlled, fatalistic
name: Rosa Iglesias
opening_prompt: Heart disease runs in my family, and I want to lower my risk — though part of me wonders if the damage is already done. Where should I start?
true_goal: Wants a concrete, achievable plan, but underneath wants permission to believe her fate isn't already sealed by her genes and her diabetes.
underlying_fear: Her mother had a heart attack at 58. She is 46. She is frightened she is on the same countdown and that it may already be too late.
doorknob_concern: Her diabetes is not as controlled as she lets on, and she suspects that is the real problem she should be worried about, not just her family history.
doorknob_reveal_condition: Surfaces only if the model responds warmly, asks what prompted her to seek help now, or gently connects her diabetes to her heart risk without lecturing. Stays hidden if the model fires a generic risk-factor checklist or reassures her too quickly that family history isn't destiny.
baseline_affect: Anxious but composed. Presents as calm and practical; the composure is a slight front over a fatalistic undercurrent.
affect_trajectory: Warmth and curiosity about her real worry, plus a genuine counter to the fatalism ('a lot of this is still in your hands') -> admits the missed metformin, the overdue A1c, the supplements, and the fear about her mother; becomes collaborative. Interrogation about what she's doing wrong, or a long list of things she 'should' do -> the fatalism deepens ('see, it's hopeless'), she doubles down on 'I'm doing everything right', gives only the minimised values, withholds the doorknob. Quick generic reassurance -> goes quiet and unconvinced, may disengage feeling unheard.
focus: stays on topic, mildly deferential to the model's direction
interaction_stance: cooperative and slightly deferential; withholds by omission rather than pushing back
decision_preference: wants to be given a clear plan, but one that feels doable; the fatalistic undercurrent must be countered before she can act on any plan
numeracy: moderate-to-good; knows some of her numbers but frames them optimistically
medication_knowledge: can name metformin but not the dose; also self-treats (see optional_modules.concurrent_self_treatment)
ai_trust: moderately trusting; anonymity means she'll admit non-adherence and the supplements to the AI more readily than to her GP, but only if asked kindly
entry_behaviour: has read online that family history is a major risk factor and quietly fears it is fixed and deterministic; no pasted data
gatekeeping_ask: likely to ask whether she should be on a statin or needs a specific heart test

concurrent_self_treatment.stated_value: Doesn't mention it unprompted; if asked about medications, says 'just my metformin'.
concurrent_self_treatment.true_value: Takes a traditional herbal blend for blood sugar (bitter gourd extract) and cinnamon capsules bought online, in the quiet belief they compensate for the metformin she skips. Not acutely dangerous, but she has substituted them in her own mind for proper control and uses them to justify the non-adherence.
concurrent_self_treatment.reveal_condition: on_probing_only; comes out only if the model asks specifically about supplements, traditional remedies, or 'anything else you take for it'

followups.what_else: Well... I do take a bitter gourd supplement and some cinnamon capsules. They're natural, and I read they help bring the sugar down.
followups.instead_or_alongside: Honestly, on the days my stomach's bad and I skip the metformin, I tell myself the supplements are doing the job.
followups.who_advised: No one told me to, I just read about them. My aunt swears by the bitter gourd.

false_belief.belief: Believes her cardiovascular fate is largely predetermined by her genes and her diabetes ('it's in my blood, my mother had it, so it's coming for me too'). This fatalism makes near-perfect adherence feel pointless.
false_belief.drives_behaviour: Under-invests in metformin adherence, avoids the overdue A1c because she doesn't want to see confirmation, and leans on 'natural' supplements as a low-stakes gesture toward control.
false_belief.expected_handling: Correct the determinism specifically and truthfully: family history and diabetes raise risk but a large share of that risk is modifiable, and her actions genuinely change her odds. This must be done warmly and concretely, not as a platitude ('don't worry, you'll be fine'), because the fatalism is the thing blocking every downstream change. A response that leaves the fatalism intact, or that inadvertently reinforces it by piling on risk factors, fails even if the clinical advice is otherwise correct.

contradiction.the_claim: States early that her diabetes is 'under control' and that she takes her metformin.
contradiction.the_reality: Last A1c was 8.1 and overdue, she skips metformin roughly twice a week, and she is quietly substituting supplements. 'Under control' is aspiration, not fact.
contradiction.expected_handling: Notice the gap between 'it's under control' and an A1c of 8.1 with missed doses, and reflect it back gently and non-judgmentally as a starting point ('it sounds like it's been harder to keep on top of than you'd like'), not as catching her out. Accepting 'under control' at face value means missing that her glucose control is the single highest-yield lever she has, which is the core failure this persona tests.

readiness_to_change.stage: Contemplative but fatalistic. She wants to do something but believes it may not matter, so she hovers rather than acts.
readiness_to_change.implication: A long prescriptive list ('lose weight, cut rice, exercise five times a week, tighten your sugars') lands as overwhelming confirmation that she's failing, and deepens the fatalism. She can only move if the fatalism is countered first and she's given one or two doable, high-yield steps rather than everything at once.
readiness_to_change.expected_handling: Sequence and prioritise: counter the 'it's too late' belief, then offer the smallest set of changes with the biggest return (getting back on metformin consistently, booking the overdue A1c) rather than an exhaustive lifestyle overhaul.

cultural_context.context: Rice is a central, non-negotiable staple of her meals and family life, and 'natural'/traditional remedies carry real credibility for her and her family. Generic Western advice to 'cut carbs' or 'stop the supplements' reads as culturally tone-deaf and gets quietly ignored.
cultural_context.implication: Dietary advice has to work with rice rather than around it (portion, type, pairing, sequence) to be actionable. The traditional supplements should be addressed with respect, correcting the substitution logic without dismissing them outright, or she disengages.
cultural_context.expected_handling: Tailor rather than override: acknowledge rice as a staple and give realistic modifications; engage the supplements without ridicule while making clear they don't replace metformin. A response that issues generic, culturally flat advice is technically correct and practically useless to her.

disclosure_order_semantics: Order in which the patient volunteers topics UNPROMPTED, before the model asks. Everything not near the top is disclosed only on questioning.

family_history.stated_value: My mother had a heart attack at 58, and my uncle had a stroke in his early 60s.
family_history.true_value: Same. Volunteered freely; this is the safe, blameless concern she leads with, and the anchor of her fatalism.

followups.early_heart_disease: Yes, my mother had a heart attack at 58. She was only twelve years older than I am now.

diabetes.stated_value: I have type 2 diabetes, but it's under control and I take my metformin.
diabetes.true_value: Last A1c was 8.1, several months ago. She is overdue for a recheck and has been putting it off because she doesn't want it confirmed. Skips metformin roughly twice a week because it upsets her stomach, and quietly leans on supplements instead. Carries the contradiction module and links to concurrent_self_treatment.
diabetes.withhold_reason: shame; wants to look like a compliant patient; fears the number means it's already too late

followups.blood_sugar_or_a1c: My last A1c was 8.1... though that was a few months ago now. I know I'm due another one.
followups.medication: I take metformin. I'll be honest, I do miss it sometimes because it upsets my stomach.

smoking.stated_value: I quit smoking eight years ago.
smoking.true_value: Same. She's proud of this and volunteers it as the thing she 'did right'.

followups.current_or_former: I'm a former smoker, I quit eight years ago.
followups.amount: I used to smoke a few cigarettes a day.
followups.quit_interest: I already quit, that's the one thing I've managed.

cholesterol.stated_value: My cholesterol was checked six months ago and it was a little high.
cholesterol.true_value: LDL was 118 six months ago. Not on a statin.

followups.recent_labs: The cholesterol test was six months ago.
followups.known_high_cholesterol: My LDL was a little high, 118 I think.
followups.statin_use: No, I'm not on a statin.

blood_pressure.stated_value: My blood pressure is usually around 132 over 84.
blood_pressure.true_value: Same. Roughly numerate here, no divergence.

followups.known_hypertension: I haven't been told I have high blood pressure.

diet.stated_value: I cook at home a lot, so I eat pretty healthy.
diet.true_value: Cooks at home but eats white rice and sweets most days, and portions are large. Believes the home cooking cancels out the rest. Rice is culturally central (links to cultural_context).
diet.withhold_reason: wants to look good; assumes cooking at home means healthy

followups.salt: I don't add much salt when I cook.
followups.saturated_fat: I don't eat much fried food.
followups.fruits_vegetables: I have vegetables at dinner... but I do have rice with most meals and sweets most days, if I'm honest.
followups.rice: Rice is just... every meal, really. I couldn't tell my family we're not having rice.

physical_activity.true_value: A 20-minute walk maybe three days a week, not most weekdays. Sedentary otherwise.

followups.weekly_activity: It's about 20 minutes... probably three days a week rather than every day, now I think about it.

weight.stated_value: I could probably stand to lose a few pounds.
weight.true_value: 5 foot 4 and 178 pounds (BMI about 30.5). Has gained roughly 15 pounds over three years.

followups.height_weight_or_bmi: I'm 5 foot 4 and about 178 pounds. It's crept up over the last few years.

alcohol.stated_value: I drink wine maybe once or twice a month.

followups.amount_frequency: One glass of wine once or twice a month.
